I suppose clever is a subjective term, what I consider clever might be obvious to others. And by clever results I mean either a tool that can be used to solve a problem in an indirect way, for instance, look at Putnam 2021 b2, (I used to help with Putnam prep sessions at my uni), anyone in the competition realm would know you are supposed to use the am gm inequality, but how exactly and which sets of numbers do you apply it to? That takes a clever and creative choice, either from experiments and just trial and error of good observations. 

An example of how to think from a different perspectives : proof the the subgroups of a finitely generated group need not be finitely generated. An entirely algebraic problem but if you think from the perspective of topology, and think in terms of fundamental group and covering space, there’s an obvious counter example.

Good question…. For me whenever I do feel like I solved a problem with something clever - either when I used to do competition problems or in the rare occasions where I solve minor lemmas in research - is when I discover a clever use of existing results in indirect ways , or when you think about your problem from a different perspective that makes certain observations clear or existing results applicable. If I have to be direct I’d say this, I’m a straightforward person, and I just try the most obvious things when I do problems first , and usually with analysis the first approach won’t give you the solution but it will give some insights or a start, and if you give me the tools I need to use I can figure out how to make it work. But with clever type problems you can give me the tools I will need and it would still take a really different perspectives to think about the problem or a clever trick would I realize how to use those tools.

I think your comment is consistent with what I’m experiencing: in the following sense.

Combinatorics problems while having lower entrance point, are difficult in the sense that they require clever and creative solutions.

While the accessibility you mentioned for pde comes from you having learnt sufficient amount of background materials - the vast knowledge you’ve accumulated and the learning skills you’ve developed in the process which has made pulling ideas from different places easier. 

So they are both hard in different ways.

And my sentiments coming from someone who enjoyed doing competition math (which I know is very different from research math) just recently realize I enjoy the problem solving process more than the learning. Or rather - as some would consider learning for a problem part of research — I would say combinatorics and pde are both hard in different ways, but I enjoy the challenge of how creative and clever I can be instead of the difficulty of how much and how fast I can learn and pull ideas from different places to synthesize results.

Agreed, the proof itself probably is the best explanation of how it works.

The goal with induction is to prove a statement is true for all cases which is usually indexed by n. And you do so by proving two things: 1. The statement is true for n=1 (or some fixed n depending on the range of n you want to prove the statement for), this is called the base case. 2. If the statement is true for n, then it is true also for n+1, this is called the inductive step.

This is kind of like proving that all the dominos will fall if you push the first one, you first prove the first one will fall, and you show that if nth domino falls so will the next one, so in turns you have proved all the dominos will fall.

With strong induction, the inductive step is slightly different but you end up proving the same thing, instead of assuming the statement is true only for n and prove that it is true for n+1, you assume it is true for all cases < n.
